title_en: Mexico and China agree to create working group to boost trade
content_en:
Economy chief Marcelo ‌Ebrard has called ‌for steps to narrow the gap needed for Mexico ‌to export agricultural and food products to China.
Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China on Thursday. Photo: AFP
Mexico and China agreed on Monday to create a working group focused on bilateral economic priorities, Mexico’s ⁠Economy Ministry said.
Economy ministers Marcelo ‌Ebrard of Mexico and Wang Wentao of China will look at ways to boost Mexican exports to China, the ministry said.
During talks in Beijing, Ebrard ⁠highlighted a persistent trade imbalance, noting that China ‌is set to export more than US$130 billion in goods to Mexico ‌this year, compared with roughly US$10 billion ⁠in ⁠Mexican shipments to China, the ministry said.
He called ‌for steps to narrow the gap, urging Beijing to expedite ‌sanitary ‌protocols - some stalled for a decade - needed for Mexico ‌to export agricultural and food products, ⁠including beef, pork, avocados, limes, sorghum and processed ⁠seafood.
The high-level meeting followed talks last week between Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and ‌Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in southern China.
By Reuters

title_en: UK sanctions Myanmar president, military figures after genocide ruling
content_en:
The UN’s International Court of Justice last ‌week ‌ruled that ‌Myanmar committed ⁠genocide against the ⁠Muslim Rohingya minority in ‌2017.
Rohingya refugees attend a mass gathering during a visit by Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh on Friday. Photo: EPA
Britain ⁠on Monday announced sanctions against five ‌people under its Myanmar and global human rights sanctions ⁠regimes, including senior ‌members of the nation’s military.
The ‌sanctions were announced ⁠after ⁠the ‌International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled last ‌week ‌ruled that ‌Myanmar committed state-sponsored ⁠genocide against the ⁠Muslim Rohingya minority population in ‌2017.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said restrictions would be placed on Min Aung Hlaing, and four other senior military members from the country in South Asia.
Miliband also said new legislation will be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week he expelled Myanmar’s defence attache after the UN’s top court had ruled the country had committed genocide during a brutal 2017 military campaign.
Miliband told members of parliament on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week and there would be a dedicated meeting in two weeks’ time.
Speaking in the House of Commons, Miliband said: “On Thursday, we ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache, because we will not tolerate a serving representative of Myanmar’s military remaining imposed on UK soil.
“I can announce today that we have also imposed sanctions against four major generals and a brigadier general, senior military figures who oversaw troops that carried out egregious civilian killings and repression of the population across Myanmar.
“We know also that the Myanmar military has systematically used lethal air power against its own people. I do not believe the British people want any UK companies to have any links to such practices.
“So we will also introduce new legislation in the coming months to stop the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar, which is used in such horrendous attacks.”
Britain’s Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs Secretary Ed Miliband and EU ambassador Caroline Wilson at the EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium on Friday. Photo: Reuters
Miliband also announced £3 million (US$3.87 million) to help Rohingya survivors, and a further £5 million of humanitarian help to support 350,000 Rohingya and Rakhine people.
He said those affected were struggling to access clean water and were suffering from malnourishment.
As well as the UK, 13 other countries on Monday “acknowledged” the ruling by the ICJ, the UN’s highest court.
The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, Gambia and Britain said Myanmar had “violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
“We underscore that the Court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court’s decision,” they said in a joint statement.
In the ruling last week, the ICJ found about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal.
Reports included that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar’s leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, who studied in England, was deposed by Myanmar’s military in 2021.
Myanmar's deposed leader Aung San Suu Kyi (left) in 2019 and Myanmar military chief Senior General Min Aung Hlaing in 2018. Photo: AFP
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan Army were still happening.
“For this government, and I would argue for the whole international community, our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action,” Miliband said.
“We should also act cognisant of the fact that the appalling targeting of civilians by the Myanmar regime continues to this day, as does the discrimination and persecution of Rohingya and other communities.”
Miliband called for an “immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement”.
“Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again,” he said.
“In the weeks and months ahead, I promise the House the UK will do everything we can to reinvigorate the political and diplomatic efforts to secure a just and lasting end to this appalling conflict.”
Reporting by Reuters, Agence France-Presse, dpa
By Agencies

title_en: Armenian PM unveils draft constitution, key to Azerbaijan peace deal
content_en:
Nikol Pashinyan proposed a constitution dropping Karabakh claims in a bid for peace with Baku, vowing to stand down if the text is rejected.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (centre) at his Armenia Ruling Civil Contract party headquarters in June. Photo: AP
Armenian leader Nikol Pashinyan unveiled a proposed new constitution on Monday that would get rid of a claim to the Karabakh region, saying it was the only way to reach a peace deal with Azerbaijan.
The Caucasus foes spent three decades locked in a territorial conflict over the mountainous region following the fall of the Soviet Union.
In a 2023 offensive, Baku retook the Armenian-populated region, forcing a mass exodus.
It has since demanded Yerevan remove claims to Karabakh from its constitution if it wants to finalise a peace treaty.
In an address to Armenians, Pashinyan promised to finalise a peace treaty with Azerbaijan should his countrymen back the new constitution in a referendum.
He vowed to stand down if the text was rejected.
Pashinyan said the new text rejects “the logic of conflict” and said the aim of the new constitution was to “ensure peace”.
The draft deletes the preamble from 1990, which included a clause for reunification with the Nagorno-Karabakh region and called for the international recognition of the genocide of Armenians by the Ottoman Empire.
US President Donald Trump (centre) with Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev (left) and Pashinyan at the White House in Washington in August last year. Photo: Reuters
The Armenian leader also said on Monday that practical work was starting on a new road – backed by US President Donald Trump – across southern Armenia linking Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave.
The project was a core part of progress towards a peace deal, which Trump is agitating for.
Armenia’s opposition has accused Pashinyan of bowing to Azerbaijan’s demands under pressure.
It has dubbed the new text “Aliyev’s Constitution” – after Azerbaijani leader Ilham Aliyev.
But Pashinyan told Armenians not to believe “that we are doing this for someone else under external pressure”.
Pashinyan – whose party is several seats short of a constitutional majority in parliament – called on the opposition not to block the referendum.
“If the people will vote against the constitution, I will resign,” he said.
Armenians call the region Artsakh and view it as their ancestral home, part of the ancient kingdom of Armenia that was populated by their ancestors 2,000 years ago.
Azerbaijan traces the history of its Muslim and Turkic tribes in the region to the Middle Ages.
The region was made part of Azerbaijan in Soviet times and following the Soviet collapse, it has been internationally recognised as part of Azerbaijan.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: UK’s former prince Andrew took ‘bribe’ to help Turkish heiress, UK court told
content_en:
Nebahat Isbilen, the wife of a jailed ex-Turkish MP, told London’s High Court she paid Andrew nearly US$1M to help her obtain UK residency.
Britain’s Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly Prince Andrew. Photo: AP
Britain’s former prince Andrew received £750,000 (US$976,000) as an alleged “bribe” to help a Turkish heiress, the High Court in London was told on Monday, with the disgraced British royal due to testify in the civil trial.
The claim around the payment emerged at the start of the anticipated four-month trial, which pits Nebahat Isbilen, whose family founded the Evyap soap and cosmetics group, against her former adviser and businessman, Selman Turk.
Isbilen, the wife of a jailed Turkish former MP, is suing Turk, alleging he misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her funds and did not explain where the money went, which he denies.
Andrew, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and who is not accused of wrongdoing, returned the £750,000 after Isbilen wrote to him at the start of the legal proceedings several years ago, according to her legal submissions.
However, he is expected to give evidence on December 14, after the judge hearing the case earlier this year permitted Turk to issue him with a witness summons, compelling him to appear at the trial.
The former prince is the first member of Britain’s royal family since 1870 to receive a summons requiring him to give High Court evidence, according to The Times.
It is the latest humiliation for King Charles’ younger brother, who was last year stripped of his royal titles following revelations stemming from his friendship with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The legal battle between Isbilen, 81, and Turk has been waged in Britain’s courts for several years and has spotlighted the involvement of Andrew and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, in various financial dealings connected to the case.
[embedded media]
Isbilen’s legal filings claim Turk sent about £2 million to a company called Alphabet Capital, some of which was transferred to Andrew and his ex-wife.
Isbilen has claimed she turned to Turk for help to get her fortune out of Turkey after her husband was jailed in 2015 on what he says were politically motivated charges.
She alleges Turk “lied to her” about the purpose of the £750,000 payment to Andrew.
But Turk’s lawyer, Joshua Hitchens, wrote in legal submissions unveiled on Monday that “her own case is that she understood that the payment to the Duke of York was a bribe, either for assistance with her passport or her UK residency”.
Hitchens goes on to claim the payment was really about discussing “her husband’s case” with Andrew, detailing a December 2019 dinner at Turk’s London flat requested by Isbilen and attended by the former Duke and Duchess of York.
“She cannot have believed that the £750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa,” Hitchens stated.
“The payment was what Mr Turk told the bank it was: a gift, made in the hope of Mr Mountbatten-Windsor taking steps to assist her husband.”
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Burnham to ignore ‘stuck in the past’ ex-PMs as he hails UK’s EU reset
content_en:
Former Conservative leaders including Rishi Sunak, Theresa May, David Cameron, and Boris Johnson warned against reopening Brexit divisions.
Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham at parliament in Westminster, London on Monday. Photo: PRU / AFP
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham accused predecessors who have warned him against reigniting the Brexit debate of being “stuck in the past” on Monday, as he trumpeted his EU reset deal.
Burnham has in recent weeks smashed a general consensus that Britain’s acrimonious departure from the European Union was done and dusted, floating the possibility that Britain could apply to rejoin.
The comments have seen pro-Brexit voices from the 2016 EU referendum reorganise to prepare for probable looming battles over Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc.
In recent days, former Conservative prime ministers Rishi Sunak, Theresa May, David Cameron and Boris Johnson have all urged Labour leader Burnham not to reopen old wounds.
“I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal,” Burnham told broadcasters.
“They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did.”
In Brussels on Friday, Burnham and the EU’s top officials sealed agreements to ease trade and youth mobility, although they kicked down the road tricky disagreements over British university fees for EU students.
The UK government argues the deals will eventually add £17 billion (US$22 billion) to Britain’s economy per annum, easing cost-of-living pressures and providing opportunities for young people.
Former British prime minister Rishi Sunak. Photo: AP
“I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills,” Burnham said.
“All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union.
“I believe it will be better for Britain to take this path and I won’t be listening to those voices who put us here in the first place,” he added.
Sunak, premier from 2022 to 2024, told Sky News that restarting the “divisive” Brexit debate would become an “all-consuming” distraction for Burnham’s government.
In an interview with the BBC, May – whose 2016 to 2019 tenure was dominated by her failure to pass a Brexit deal – urged Burnham to “accept Brexit and move on”.
It echoed warnings from Cameron, who called the referendum and resigned following the result, and Johnson, who took Britain out of the bloc in early 2020.
The comments evoked the so-called Brexit wars that dominated political discourse for years following the narrow vote.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch at the annual conference of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) in London, Britain on Monday. Photo: EPA
On Monday, Nigel Farage, the leader of the anti-EU Reform UK party, was expected to say that “going backwards into the EU’s orbit would be a disaster for the very British businesses that are trying to compete and innovate”, according to excerpts released by his office.
Meanwhile, Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch said rejoining the EU “is not going to fix” Britain’s stagnant economy.
Burnham’s office said he would tell parliament in an afternoon speech that Friday’s agreements mean there is a “very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through”.
Burnham intends to discuss with Brussels options for future ties with the EU over the next 12 months. He has said the British public will be “the boss” over the future relationship, but has not said whether this means another referendum.
He has ruled out free movement or rejoining the single market or customs union during this parliament, which will end when he calls a general election, expected in 2029.
Several Labour MPs have praised Burnham for breaking the taboo over Brexit and have said he should put rejoining in the party’s next manifesto, but the party is divided.
By Agence France-Presse

It echoed warnings from Cameron, who called the referendum and resigned following the result, and Johnson, who took Britain out of the bloc in early 2020.
The comments evoked the so-called Brexit wars that dominated political discourse for years following the narrow vote.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch at the annual conference of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) in London, Britain on Monday. Photo: EPA
On Monday, Nigel Farage, the leader of the anti-EU Reform UK party, was expected to say that “going backwards into the EU’s orbit would be a disaster for the very British businesses that are trying to compete and innovate”, according to excerpts released by his office.
Meanwhile, Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch said rejoining the EU “is not going to fix” Britain’s stagnant economy.
Burnham’s office said he would tell parliament in an afternoon speech that Friday’s agreements mean there is a “very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through”.
Burnham intends to discuss with Brussels options for future ties with the EU over the next 12 months. He has said the British public will be “the boss” over the future relationship, but has not said whether this means another referendum.
He has ruled out free movement or rejoining the single market or customs union during this parliament, which will end when he calls a general election, expected in 2029.
Several Labour MPs have praised Burnham for breaking the taboo over Brexit and have said he should put rejoining in the party’s next manifesto, but the party is divided.

title_en: UK Grand Theft Auto VI hacker gets 7-year sentence
content_en:
Arion Kurtaj, 21, walked free from a London court on time served after pleading guilty to the 2021–2022 Rockstar Games hacks.
Grand Theft Auto VI was released last week. Photo: Reuters
A UK court sentenced a British hacker to seven years in prison on Monday for a series of cyberattacks, including leaking footage from Grand Theft Auto VI years before the blockbuster game’s release.
Having already served years in custody, Arion Kurtaj, aged 21, was entitled to walk free immediately, Judge Mark Turner said at London’s Woolwich Crown Court.
Kurtaj, who is autistic, pleaded guilty last week to hacking major companies between 2021 and 2022, including Grand Theft Auto-maker Rockstar Games, mobile operator BT/EE, digital bank Revolut and ride-hailing giant Uber.
Turner described the offences as “sophisticated attacks upon big companies”.
“Don’t let this happen again,” he added.
The judge said his sentencing decision required “balancing the seriousness of what you did with, on the other hand, your young age” and medical diagnoses.
[embedded media]
Kurtaj was a teenager when he carried out the attacks as a key member of the so-called Lapsus$ hacking group.
He was initially charged over hacking BT/EE and placed in a hotel for his own protection from rival hackers in September 2022, according to the Crown Prosecution Service.
But from his hotel room, he went on to carry out cyberattacks on Revolut, Uber and Rockstar.
Using just a mobile phone, the hotel’s wifi-connected television and an Amazon Fire TV Stick, he broke into Rockstar systems and obtained 90 videos of the highly anticipated GTA VI game.
He leaked the videos online under the username “TeaPotUberHacker”, more than a year before the first official footage was released by Rockstar, causing a frenzy across the video game industry.
The hack disrupted the release strategy for the sixth instalment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, which was finally released last week after a 13-year wait.
In 2023, a jury concluded that Kurtaj, whom psychiatrists at the time had deemed unfit to stand trial, was responsible for numerous computer misuse, fraud and blackmail offences.
Due to the severity of his autism, he was placed under a hospital order where he remained for two years before being found fit to stand trial, his lawyers said.

title_en: Nato vows space defence after Russia nuclear satellite report
content_en:
German media reported that Moscow is planning a launch within weeks that would give it the ability to destroy satellites.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (right) and Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte at the Chancellery in Berlin, Germany on Monday. Photo: EPA
Nato chief Mark Rutte said on Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space when asked about German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
The media reports, citing unnamed German military and BND spy agency sources, said Moscow was thought to be planning such a launch in the coming weeks, giving it the capability to destroy other satellites.
Rutte, asked about the reports while visiting Berlin, vowed: “We will always make sure that we defend every inch of Nato territory and that includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking alongside Rutte, did not confirm or deny the media reports but voiced concern.
“Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking,” he said.
“They reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue,” added Merz, whose chancellery oversees the BND foreign intelligence agency.
A German government spokesman earlier said that the reports were being taken “very seriously,” though he did not confirm them either and warned against causing “excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers”.
[embedded media]
Public broadcasters WDR and NDR, along with the Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, reported that Russia planned to launch a satellite dubbed “Sputnik-S” equipped with a nuclear warhead some time in the coming weeks.
The outlets, citing unnamed sources, said the intelligence reports about the plans had recently been shared among several Nato countries and that the German government had been briefed on the matter.
The satellite had been stored in the Moscow region, according to the news outlets, and could be used to disrupt or destroy important communications and observation satellites orbiting Earth.
The BND declined to comment when questioned by Agence France-Presse, while the German military’s space command pointed to general remarks from Defence Minister Boris Pistorius that threats in outer space are being taken seriously.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the latest news stories on the topic but that frequent reports citing “unknown sources” are “hardly worth taking seriously”.
Josef Aschbacher, head of the European Space Agency, described the presence of nuclear weapons in space as “the ultimate nightmare scenario” in comments to the Handelsblatt newspaper.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Fresh faces in Election Committee: how will they affect the chief executive race?
content_en:
A 99 per cent turnout and 500 fresh faces reshape the Election Committee, though analysts say it’s too early to call John Lee’s odds.
Elected Election Committee candidates in the catering subsector pose on stage at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on November 22. Photo: Sam Tsang
Newcomers are making up one-third of Hong Kong’s powerful Election Committee tasked with selecting the next city leader, with politicians and analysts saying the influx of fresh faces could bring new policy perspectives to next year’s chief executive race and strengthen post-election oversight.
A South China Morning Post tally found that at least 482 returning members of the 1,500-seat electoral college previously nominated John Lee Ka-chiu in 2022. But political observers said it was premature to conclude that the line-up gave him an advantage if he were to seek re-election.
Sunday’s poll returned 723 elected members, including more than 220 newcomers. Together with 259 uncontested members, 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies, the full committee now includes 500 new faces in total.
In the next term of office, whoever becomes chief executive will be expected to press on with the execution of Hong Kong’s maiden five-year blueprint amid intensifying geopolitical tensions and this makes the role of the election committee more critical.
Counting takes place at the central counting station at Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai on November 22. Photo: Sam Tsang
Senior counsel Ronny Tong Ka-wah, a member of the top decision-making Executive Council who won re-election in the legal subsector, expected the newcomers to play a more proactive role in monitoring the city leader’s performance at such a critical juncture in the city’s development.
“Beyond choosing the chief executive, I think Election Committee members also serve the function of monitoring whether the city leader delivers on his election promises,” he said.
“However, when it comes to whether the members know how to utilise different channels to carry out that oversight, it will take some time to hone those skills.”
Having several heavyweights elected to the electoral college for the first time, such as former justice secretary Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung, ex-health minister Sophia Chan Siu-chee and former innovation and technology secretary Alfred Sit Wing-hang, Tong said they would be well placed to carry out that duty and should guide the novices.
Noting that Hong Kong’s political and social environment had stabilised, Tong described the current stage as appropriate for generational succession.
He also hoped the fresh faces would bring in new perspectives when selecting the city leader and lawmakers.
“It is good to have new views, as the chief executive needs to meet the demands and views of different sectors of the public,” Tong added.
Tam Yiu-chung, a former Hong Kong deputy to the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, the country’s top legislative body, also believed the influx of new members, including industry leaders, would lead to more active engagement in the chief executive race through policy suggestions, particularly on how to implement the first five-year plan well.
With the coming chief executive race set to be consequential in charting Hong Kong’s direction, Tam said it could shift from one-way communication by candidates towards greater input and more active engagement from Election Committee members.
“I think they could give more input when discussing the manifesto,” Tam said. “Since the five-year plan is already in place, there may be more discussion on how the next chief executive can implement it.”
Selina Lau Pui-ling, chief executive of the Hong Kong Federation of Insurers, is among the industry heavyweights first to join the key body.
She credited her victory to her track record of serving the sector and said she aimed to better represent and promote the insurance industry.
“I think more newcomers have taken part in the election; I believe everyone wants to work for the industry,” Lau added.
“Insurance has been relatively overlooked. I hope that through the Election Committee, we can help the government and more people see the important value of insurance.”
The election, which posted a historic high turnout of 99 per cent, also delivered a string of surprise upsets among veteran members seeking re-election. Comparing the list of elected members with the results of the 2021 poll and the 2025 by-election, 65 incumbents were unseated.
Notable casualties included former secretary for financial services and the treasury Ceajer Chan Ka-keung and president of the Law Society of Hong Kong Roden Tong Man-lung.
Across the 31 contested subsectors, social welfare saw the fiercest competition, with 25 hopefuls vying for 15 seats. Four of seven incumbents running for re-election lost, the highest proportion across all subsectors.
Those defeated included Hong Kong Sheng Kung Hui Welfare Council deputy director Joseph Man Hung-yee and veteran social worker Agnes Yeung Law Koon-chui.
Yeung attributed her loss to strong opponents, who were mainly management-level staff from major non-governmental organisations.
“They represent large NGOs and have abundant resources and strong networks, making them easy to reach out to different parties,” Yeung said, adding that those rivals had not contested in the race five years ago.
Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing attributed the unseating of incumbents to greater uncertainty in outcomes from a larger base of voters.
However, with more voters casting their ballots this year, incumbents face tougher competition and less certainty over the election result, he added.
Supporters gather outside the Harbour Road Sports Centre polling station in Wan Chai on November 22. Photo: Karma Lo
Of the 5,709 registered voters, 5,640 cast their ballots on Sunday. Overall turnout increased by about 9 percentage points from 2021.
Lo also pointed out that the unseating of incumbents and the election of new faces showed internal competition among the patriotic elites.
“The desire for representation turnover is obvious. It is a healthy sign,” Lo said. “They do not want incumbents to count on a monopolistic tendency.”
As the Election Committee’s first major task is to nominate and choose the next chief executive early next year, many newly elected members declined to reveal whether they would support Lee for a second term, despite most praising his performance.
The nomination threshold for the chief executive race stands at 188, while Lee secured 786 in 2022. Of them, at least 482 returned as Election Committee members, while at least 26 lost re-election.
Lo said it would take time to gauge the leanings of the newly elected members, and it was too early to assess how the shake-up within the Election Committee would affect the race.
Tam, who served as the director of Lee’s campaign office in 2022, also suggested that it was premature to tell whether the new composition favoured the city leader.
“There are too many unknowns right now to discuss [the chief executive election]. We do not even know who is running; speculating on the views of Election Committee members is premature,” Tam added.
“Even if you asked those members who nominated John Lee, they may not be able to tell you [their stance] now.”
By Matthew Cheng, Jess Ma

title_en: Malaysia’s Anwar says easier to deal with China than US amid tech tensions
content_en:
In an interview, the prime minister reveals how he navigates superpower rivalry, Trump’s pro-China complaint and AI chip curbs on Malaysia.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in an interview with the South China Morning Post in Shenzhen on Friday. Photo: Nora Tam
China has never raised any concerns about Malaysia being close to the United States nor stood in the way of any technology arrangements with the Americans, the Southeast Asian country’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has said.
In an interview with the South China Morning Post in Shenzhen before a bilateral meeting with China’s President Xi Jinping, Anwar said he found Beijing easier to deal with than Washington but maintained that his government was not leaning towards one side or the other.
The recurring issue of Malaysia’s strategic hedging between the two superpowers has come under the spotlight again, as the US last week imposed curbs on advanced artificial intelligence chips to Kuala Lumpur and three other Southeast Asian nations for fear they would be used by Chinese data centres based there.
The US announcement could dampen Malaysia’s growth as a regional hub for data centres, a sector that has secured nearly US$100 billion in investments since 2021.
The country has a high concentration of Chinese-owned data centres alongside major investments by Nvidia and Google either through local partners or on their own. On November 4, Google announced a US$15 billion investment for 2027-28 to build data centres and clean energy projects, among other investments.
Speaking after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, Anwar acknowledged that his country was often portrayed as being pro-China. He revealed that Donald Trump had raised this with him when the US president visited the Malaysian capital last year.
Anwar told the SCMP: “I’ll be very frank here that it is certainly easier with the Chinese. No 1: they’re our neighbours. We’re more familiar with their culture and they are more forthcoming. For example, meeting President Xi Jinping or Premier Li Qiang is much easier. They take time to listen, to try and appreciate and understand some of our concerns.”
Anwar Ibrahim says the Malaysian government is not leaning towards China or the US. Photo: Nora Tam
Contrary to speculation, he stressed that China did not demand that Malaysia take its side against the US.
“Having excellent relations with China does not preclude us from continuing to engage with the United States. And the Chinese seem to understand. People tend to suggest that I’m tilting a bit towards China. It’s not true,” Anwar said.
Malaysia is one of seven Asean members that have joined the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), an AI governance alliance led by China.
While Malaysia has agreed to set up a “sovereign AI cloud” with the US, it has not joined Pax Silica, a US-led initiative that aims to secure supply chains for AI, semiconductors and critical minerals while reducing reliance on China. Two members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations – Singapore and the Philippines – are part of Pax Silica.
Anwar said Malaysia was “open” to the idea of joining Pax Silica and did not expect opposition from Beijing. “There was never any pressure or suggestion from China to say, ‘no, please be wary’,” Anwar said, referring to Pax Silica. “It hasn’t happened in my meetings with President Xi Jinping; I had no sense of that.”
Mainland China and Hong Kong are Malaysia’s second- and third-largest sources of annual foreign investment after Singapore. China is also Malaysia’s largest trading partner, with the US coming in third behind Singapore.
Trump reacts to dancing performers during a welcoming ceremony at Kuala Lumpur International Airport last October. Photo: AP
On Xi’s American counterpart, Anwar revealed details of his 40-minute conversation inside the US presidential limousine – the “Beast” – during Trump’s official visit to Kuala Lumpur last year for the 47th Asean summit. Anwar said Trump told him, “You are leaning towards China.”
“So I said, Mr President, we don’t have to lean. They’re just our immediate neighbour. We share the same waters and we have centuries-old relations,” Anwar said.
He said he reassured Trump that Malaysia remained a close friend of the US, reminding the US president about their bilateral trade, American investments and Anwar’s own past stint teaching at Georgetown University.
“Contrary to some other perceptions, he’s a good listener. I’m not sure whether he agreed, but he was kind. He was exceedingly kind in that discussion in the Beast,” Anwar said.
[embedded media]
On the new US restrictions, Anwar said Malaysia would monitor if American companies were somehow sending chips to China, just as it would monitor Chinese firms required to operate under Beijing’s rules.
“If you impose a condition on the [US] company that it cannot export to China, fair. We will observe that because that is the agreement you have with your company,” he said.
“But that will not preclude our decision to work with the Chinese, with Chinese investments and with Chinese companies making their own decisions.”
He said he had conveyed this message to both Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio as recently as two weeks ago.
Any foreign investor demanding dedicated government oversight to safeguard its supply chain would have to foot the bill as well, the prime minister said.
“You want our help? Yes. You pay. We are getting smart as a business,” he added.

The recurring issue of Malaysia’s strategic hedging between the two superpowers has come under the spotlight again, as the US last week imposed curbs on advanced artificial intelligence chips to Kuala Lumpur and three other Southeast Asian nations for fear they would be used by Chinese data centres based there.
The US announcement could dampen Malaysia’s growth as a regional hub for data centres, a sector that has secured nearly US$100 billion in investments since 2021.

On November 4, Google announced a US$15 billion investment for 2027-28 to build data centres and clean energy projects, among other investments.
Speaking after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, Anwar acknowledged that his country was often portrayed as being pro-China. He revealed that Donald Trump had raised this with him when the US president visited the Malaysian capital last year.
Anwar told the SCMP: “I’ll be very frank here that it is certainly easier with the Chinese. No 1: they’re our neighbours. We’re more familiar with their culture and they are more forthcoming. Mainland China and Hong Kong are Malaysia’s second- and third-largest sources of annual foreign investment after Singapore. China is also Malaysia’s largest trading partner, with the US coming in third behind Singapore.

“So I said, Mr President, we don’t have to lean. They’re just our immediate neighbour. We share the same waters and we have centuries-old relations,” Anwar said.
He said he reassured Trump that Malaysia remained a close friend of the US, reminding the US president about their bilateral trade, American investments and Anwar’s own past stint teaching at Georgetown University.
“Contrary to some other perceptions, he’s a good listener. I’m not sure whether he agreed, but he was kind. He was exceedingly kind in that discussion in the Beast,” Anwar said.
[embedded media]

“If you impose a condition on the [US] company that it cannot export to China, fair. We will observe that because that is the agreement you have with your company,” he said.

“You want our help? Yes. You pay. We are getting smart as a business,” he added.

title_en: What’s at stake and the battlegrounds to watch as Taiwan heads to the polls
content_en:
Officials will be elected across 22 cities and counties on Saturday, and all eyes are on the contests in Taipei and New Taipei City.
Supporters hold placards during a campaign rally for Taipei Mayor Wayne Chiang on November 14. Photo: AFP
Taiwan’s local elections on Saturday will test the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s political strength, the opposition’s unity and the island’s direction ahead of the 2028 leadership race.
Voters will elect officials across 22 cities and counties. But attention is focused on Taipei and New Taipei City, where closely watched contests could have significant implications for Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te and main opposition Kuomintang chairwoman Cheng Li-wun.
Adding an unexpected twist is the social media-driven “Ocean Current” campaign centred on the DPP’s mayoral candidate for Taipei, Puma Shen Pao-yang.
Analysts are divided over whether that movement will help to reshape the political landscape in Taiwan, influence the opposition’s strategy for 2028, and have wider implications for cross-strait relations.
[embedded media]
What are the nine-in-one elections?
Held every four years, Taiwan’s nine-in-one elections allow voters to choose officials for nine categories of local government posts, ranging from mayors and county commissioners to councillors and village chiefs.
About 19.65 million people are eligible to vote this year, including an estimated 600,000 first-time voters.
The most closely watched contests are for the leadership of Taiwan’s 22 cities and counties, with 81 candidates competing for the posts.
Independents form the largest group, with 34 candidates, while the KMT and DPP have each fielded 19. The smaller opposition Taiwan People’s Party has nominated just one candidate, and eight candidates are representing other minor parties.
The elections are widely regarded as a midterm test of Lai’s administration, which has repeatedly clashed with the opposition-controlled legislature.
In 2022, the KMT won 14 mayoral and county commissioner seats against the DPP’s five. Its tally subsequently rose to 15 after an independent county commissioner rejoined the party.
The DPP is seeking to expand its local government presence, while the KMT hopes to defend its strongholds and make gains in the south.
Why are Taipei and New Taipei the ones to watch?
The two northern municipalities have emerged as the most politically significant contests, particularly because of the unexpected momentum from Puma Shen’s challenge to incumbent KMT Taipei Mayor Wayne Chiang Wan-an.
Shen, a legislator and co-founder of the Kuma Academy, has been sanctioned and labelled a “diehard Taiwan separatist” by Beijing for his advocacy of civil defence against threats from mainland China.
He has drawn attention with a campaign emphasising direct voter engagement and social media mobilisation that has been dubbed the Ocean Current or yangliu – a play on his name, Pao-yang.
DPP mayoral candidate Puma Shen visits a market in Taipei on November 5. Photo: Reuters
Huang Huei-hua, director of the Taipei-based Taiwan Global Talk think tank, said Shen’s approach had energised voters to think beyond their traditional party loyalties.
“You don’t necessarily have to talk about heavy political issues all the time. Sometimes, you first need to make people feel that being with you is fun,” she said.
“That brings voters’ energy and enthusiasm back. This is what the Ocean Current phenomenon is all about.”
Huang argued that Shen’s campaign had generated momentum beyond Taipei, potentially benefiting DPP candidate Su Chiao-hui in neighbouring New Taipei City, where she faces the KMT’s Lee Shu-chuan.
New Taipei City – Taiwan’s most populous municipality with more than 4 million residents – is widely regarded as a key electoral battleground and a barometer of the island’s political direction.
The KMT has governed the area since 2005, when it was still Taipei county, making the election a test of whether the party can preserve more than two decades of control or the DPP can achieve a significant breakthrough.
With support for the DPP and KMT relatively evenly divided, the contest between Su and Lee – who has secured joint KMT-TPP backing – is expected to be closely watched.
Taipei Mayor Wayne Chiang, of the KMT, is seeking re-election. Photo: AFP
“If the KMT loses both Taipei and New Taipei, it would show that the amplification of the Ocean Current phenomenon through social media has been effective,” said Max Lo, executive director of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society.
But he warned that the movement could also undermine traditional DPP factions, whose influence depends heavily on local political networks and grass-roots organisers.
He said online mobilisation could overshadow these established organisations, creating tensions within the party even as it energised younger supporters.
What’s at stake for Lai and Cheng?
The results could have important consequences for the leadership of both major parties.
The DPP currently controls the southern municipalities of Kaohsiung and Tainan, while the KMT governs the other four.
For Lai, who also chairs the DPP, a strong performance could consolidate his authority and provide political momentum ahead of his expected re-election bid in 2028.
For Cheng, the elections represent her first major electoral test as KMT chairwoman, amid disagreements within the party over her determined push to restore dialogue and improve strained relations with Beijing.
Huang suggested that losing both Taipei and New Taipei City could threaten Cheng’s leadership and potentially prompt current Taipei mayor Chiang to seek the party chairmanship as a platform for future political ambitions.
Lo, however, cautioned against drawing conclusions from the results in two municipalities alone.
“Of the six major municipalities, if the KMT loses Taipei and New Taipei but wins Kaohsiung while retaining Taichung and Taoyuan, would that really constitute an electoral defeat?” he asked.
Supporters wave flags during a rally for DPP mayoral candidate Puma Shen in Taipei on November 15. Photo: AFP
Can the KMT and TPP work together?
The elections will also test cooperation between the KMT and TPP, whose failed attempt to form a joint ticket exposed deep divisions within the opposition ahead of the 2024 leadership election.
Although TPP chairman Huang Kuo-chang withdrew from the New Taipei City mayoral race and backed the KMT candidate, nomination disputes in places such as Zhubei have highlighted lingering tensions.
Lo said the two parties nevertheless had strong incentives to maintain their alliance ahead of 2028.
“If the blue [KMT] and white [TPP] camps split, they will lose. Only by cooperating will they have a chance of winning in 2028,” he said.
Could the vote affect ties with Beijing?
The Taipei contest has attracted particular attention because Shen has been placed on Beijing’s list of “diehard Taiwan independence separatists”.
Beijing has also imposed sanctions on businesses linked to his father.
But Shen has said he would consider continuing the annual Taipei-Shanghai Twin-City Forum – an exchange event between the two governments – if elected, provided there were no political preconditions or harassment.
He also argued that the election would represent a victory for Taiwan’s democracy regardless of who won, because voters remained free to choose their leaders despite Beijing’s pressure.
Huang said Beijing would be displeased by a Shen victory, and that could potentially contribute to a further deterioration in cross-strait relations.
Lo said if Shen did get elected, Beijing might respond with military exercises or joint patrols but was unlikely to fundamentally change its broader strategy towards Taiwan.
Wang Kung-yi, head of the Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, cautioned against interpreting local election results mainly through the prism of cross-strait confrontation.
He said the KMT’s electoral fortunes should not automatically be equated with Beijing’s political interests.
“The KMT has its own supporters, political traditions and foundations in local governance in Taiwan. It is not an appendage of Beijing’s political strategy,” Wang said.
He stressed that DPP victories in Taipei and New Taipei City would not necessarily signify public endorsement of its cross-strait policies, just as KMT defeats would not mean voters had rejected closer exchanges with Beijing.
Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
Will the results determine the 2028 race?
Although Saturday’s vote could redirect political momentum, analysts said the local election results should not be viewed as a definitive guide to 2028.
Wang argued that voters could support one party’s local candidates while backing another party in an island-wide leadership contest.
He said economic conditions, energy policy, cross-strait risks, defence spending and governing competence would ultimately play a greater role in shaping the 2028 election.
Lo agreed that the political environment could change significantly over the next two years.
“Whether these issues will actually affect the 2028 election depends on the political trends and the strength of public sentiment at that time,” he said.
For Wang, the more immediate question was whether candidates could deliver better local governance rather than claim a political victory over Beijing.
By Lawrence Chung

title_en: Israel leadership rivals clash over Iran threat ahead of coalition talks
content_en:
Gadi Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a new government to replace Netanyahu after October’s vote failed to give either bloc a majority.
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party arrives to speak at the Knesset, Israel’s parliament in Jerusalem on Monday. Photo: Reuters
Gadi Eisenkot, who is tasked with forming the next Israeli government, said he saw no immediate reason for attacking Iran on Monday, contradicting caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who warned against downplaying “grave threats”.
The remarks from both politicians came hours before their parties were due to meet for the third time to discuss possible coalition-building, after lengthy negotiations the day before delivered no breakthrough.
Eisenkot has until December 6 – a deadline which can be extended by 14 days – to form a government to replace Netanyahu after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc.
The former military chief’s wide-ranging camp faces divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a national unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud.
Netanyahu has repeatedly pressed for a unity government, which he says is needed to guarantee Israel’s security.
During a press briefing at Israel’s parliament in Jerusalem on Monday, Eisenkot said the “Iranian threat is the most serious threat to the State of Israel”.
“But at this moment I do not see a direct and immediate threat to the State of Israel that would require action before a government is formed,” he added.
Netanyahu in turn played up the need for unity “in the face of the great threats surrounding us”.
“Anyone who belittles or downplays these immediate, serious and grave threats surrounding us does so for political reasons,” he said in televised remarks.
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a Likud party meeting at the Knesset in Jerusalem on Monday. Photo: dpa
Delegations from Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party and Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud are due to meet on Monday evening for a third round of negotiations, spokespeople for Likud and Yashar told Agence France-Presse earlier on Monday.
Representatives from each party met for four hours on Sunday and laid out their positions “on a range of substantive issues”, but with no sign of a breakthrough.
On Saturday, Yashar presented the talks as “a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government”, saying that Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options.
Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, including an end to “all personal attacks” and political “boycotts” targeting Netanyahu and his government.
Eisenkot’s 48-member bloc needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority and remains divided over how to build a coalition. Short of 61 lawmakers, Eisenkot’s bloc could form a minority government.
In parliament on Monday, Yair Golan, who heads the left-leaning Democrats party which is a part of Eisenkot’s camp, said: “We will not agree to any unity government with Netanyahu”.
Yair Golan, of the Democrats party, speaks at the Knesset in Jerusalem on Monday. Photo: Reuters
Earlier on social media, Golan had urged an end to the “sham talks with Likud”. He has instead called for an alliance with the Arab-majority lists, which won record gains in the October vote.
Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.
Such an arrangement could allow Netanyahu to keep his political leverage against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.
But that prospect runs up against Eisenkot’s refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign.
Last week, Eisenkot said that he would be prepared to put forward a minority national emergency government for a parliamentary vote should efforts to create a broad-based government fail.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Trump targets Newsom and Democrats in Justice Department speech focused on violent crime
content_en:
The US president condemned the ‘radical left’ and the California governor’s decision to commute hundreds of death sentences in the state.
US President Donald Trump speaks at the Justice Department in Washington on Monday. Photo: AFP
US President Donald Trump condemned California Governor Gavin Newsom’s decision to commute hundreds of death sentences in the state, using a Justice Department visit to sharply chastise an outspoken Democratic critic who is considering his own bid for the White House.
The speech, Trump’s second address at the department in less than two years, offered the president a platform to showcase what he said was his administration’s success in combating violent crime as he repeatedly veered into partisan politics while trying to draw a contrast with Newsom and a Democratic Party he cast as part of a “radical left”.
“For years now, we have watched the radical left commit one betrayal of justice and safety after another,” Trump said in a speech that was also interspersed with first-person accounts from relatives of victims of crimes affected by Newsom’s clemency.
Newsom has said the decision this month to commute the sentences of more than 500 inmates to punishments of life in prison without parole was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families. The state’s Supreme Court would be required to approve most those commutations.
“I won’t take lectures on accountability from a president who has used the pardon power to help wealthy friends and business associates avoid accountability while victims are left fighting to recover what was stolen from them. Justice should be about the people we serve, not the political interests of the people in power,” Newsom said in a statement about Trump’s speech.
Trump has long sought to position himself as a tough-on-crime president who staunchly backs law enforcement. He has taken credit for the dropping of violent crime rates that experts say have been declining since 2022.

title_en: US says detained Princeton PhD student from China overstayed visa in 2016
content_en:
Department of Homeland Security claims Chinese scholar Eva Yi Xie never had authorisation to study in the US.
Princeton University in New Jersey. Eva Yi Xie is a third-year PhD student at the prestigious Ivy League institution and researches the neural basis of decision-making. Photo: Shutterstock
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has said a Chinese PhD student at Princeton University in New Jersey, detained by immigration authorities last week, overstayed her authorised period of stay in the country in 2016.
A DHS spokesperson told the South China Morning Post on Monday that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) carried out a “targeted immigration enforcement operation” at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington on November 19 to arrest Eva Yi Xie.
Xie was admitted to the US on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, but failed to leave by the required date of September 15 that year, the spokesperson said.
“Xie has NEVER held valid authorisation to study in the United States. To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
DHS did not specify which application it meant. Xie “will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings”, the spokesperson added.
[embedded media]
Xie’s lawyer, Kerry Doyle, told media outlets that her client is seeking asylum. Her parents filed an asylum application on her behalf within a year of her arrival in the US, Doyle told The Daily Princetonian.
The application was referred to immigration court, where Xie reportedly has a hearing scheduled for January 2028. Princeton University arranged her legal representation.
Doyle did not immediately respond to SCMP’s requests for comment.
Xie, a third-year PhD student, researches the neural basis of decision-making. She graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics, and has interned at Meta Platforms, Microsoft AI and IBM Research.
A 2020 profile in the student newspaper of New York’s Bronx High School of Science said Xie moved from Shanghai to the US in 2016 following what she described as an “overnight decision”. She was a finalist that year in the Regeneron Science Talent Search, a national competition for high school students.
In a 2020 account published on the Society for Science website, Xie wrote that when she was 14, her parents were “compelled to flee to America to seek refuge after being politically persecuted”.
The case has attracted widespread attention on Chinese social media, where users have circulated claims about Xie’s parents. SCMP could not independently verify those claims.
From February to July 2025, over 1,000 Chinese nationals were booked into ICE detention – more than five times the number detained during the year earlier period, according to AAPI Data, the UCLA Asian-American Studies Centre and Stop AAPI Hate.
And for the full 2025 financial year, ICE deported 3,226 Chinese nationals, a 524 per cent increase over fiscal 2024 levels.
Boyfriend describes Xie as a ‘brilliant’ neuroscientist
Xie’s boyfriend, Rupert Li, a doctoral student in mathematics at Stanford University in California, told The Daily Princetonian that at the time of her arrest, Xie was planning to take a domestic flight to San Francisco International Airport to visit him.
He posted on Instagram that he was upset about Xie’s arrest.
“Eva is a brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist, and a caring and loving partner,” he said. “Please help us bring her home.”
Court records show that Xie filed a habeas corpus petition on November 20 in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, alleging that she was being unlawfully detained. A judge ordered the government not to remove Xie from the district while the case was pending and directed it to respond by 5pm on Wednesday.
The judge has not ruled on the legality of Xie’s detention. If the government files a response opposing her petition, Xie must reply by November 30.
ICE’s online detainee locator lists a Yi Xie, born in China, at the Caroline Detention Facility in Virginia, matching the Princeton student’s name and country of birth.
By Han Li, Zhang Tong

title_en: Germans reject choosing between US and China as faith in the West crumbles
content_en:
Bipartisan desire for neutrality comes as a major new survey also reveals anxiety about the economic threat posed by Beijing.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Germany’s President Frank-Walter Steinmeier in Beijing on October 30. A new survey has revealed Germans' anxiety about the economic threat China poses. Photo: EPA
Amid heated superpower rivalry, a vast majority of Germans want to remain neutral between the United States and China, even as a major new survey also reveals anxiety about the economic threat posed by Beijing.
The Berlin Pulse, an annual survey, showed that 83 per cent do not want to pick a side between the world’s two foremost powers. Just two per cent wished to side with China, compared with 15 per cent for the US.
The desire for neutrality spanned party lines and demographics, and respondents also believed Europe should stand up for itself. More than two-thirds (68 per cent) said the bloc was “too restrained” in defending its economic interests against the US, while 59 per cent felt the same way about China.
The poll comes at a delicate moment for Europe, which was not offered a seat at the table for last week’s talks between the leaders of China, the US and Russia in Shenzhen. Its absence fuelled a sense of anxiety that the bloc, which trails the US and China in technological terms, was being left behind.
This disillusionment has helped the extreme-right Alternative for Germany party rise in the polls and outperform mainstream parties in recent state elections.
[embedded media]
In the Berlin Pulse, 61 per cent of respondents say that the “West no longer exists as a political and cultural unity between Europe and the US”, illustrating how the transatlantic divorce, playing out at the top level of politics, has percolated through the voter base.
More than two-thirds (77 per cent) described relations with the US as “rather/very bad”, up from 73 per cent a year earlier. The number of respondents who viewed the US as a partner on Ukraine has halved in two years to 35 per cent, while just one-quarter of those quizzed believed it a partner in “dealing with China”.
The poll captures mixed views on China, at a time of great flux in the bilateral relationship. The government in Berlin is pivoting towards a more hawkish stance towards China, as it fears its manufacturing sector being hollowed out by Chinese competition.
It has thrown its support behind more hard-line trade measures, including a “kill switch” set to be unveiled on December 9, that could close the EU market to countries seen as engaging in coercive behaviour.
In total, 90 per cent of Germans polled described China as a threat to the economy, with 60 per cent seeing it as a “major threat”. Conversely, negative perceptions of Beijing’s growing global influence have fallen from 61 per cent in 2024 to 43 per cent today, suggesting that Germans are becoming less hostile towards China’s global rise, even as they regard its economic power as threatening.
In military terms, 46 per cent saw China as a threat – although just seven per cent as a major one. This threat perception has, however, been falling, down from 55 per cent last year.
[embedded media]
Meanwhile, just two per cent believed China was Germany’s most important “foreign policy interest”, while support for Taiwan, among the EU’s biggest members, is also cratering. Two years ago, 31 per cent of Germans would have supported German military help to Taipei in a conflict with Beijing. This has fallen to 17 per cent today.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited – by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and all EU members, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
The results suggest Germans believe they are sandwiched between two powers who pose some level of threat. As a marker of how quickly things have changed in the West, respondents were not even asked whether the US posed a military threat last year; now 37 per cent believe it does.
They also suggest a general ambivalence with what were until recently mainstream policies. Starkly, support for Ukraine has plummeted – with just 46 per cent saying Germany should militarily support Kyiv, down from 59 per cent a year earlier.
Strikingly, when asked who Germany’s most important foreign policy partner is, just four per cent said the European Union – which polled at the same level as Russia and China. France led with 40 per cent, followed by the US at 24 per cent.
By Finbarr Bermingham

title_en: US states sue Musk companies over flood of sexualised images made with AI chatbot Grok
content_en:
Democratic attorneys general in Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday, accusing the firms of promoting Grok’s ‘spicy mode’.
Elon Musk and screens displaying the logo of AI chatbot Grok. Photo: AFP
Elon Musk’s businesses harmed consumers by avoiding safeguards when they designed and launched an artificial intelligence chatbot capable of creating sexualised images, two Democratic attorneys general argued in lawsuits filed on Monday.
The choices that went into building Grok led to a proliferation of child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual intimate imagery on the companies’ platforms, the lawsuits said. The companies prioritised their business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit.
“To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity,” Jones said in the lawsuit. “For these defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.”
Oregon also filed a lawsuit on Monday. The attorneys general brought their separate but similar cases under their states’ consumer protection statutes.
The lawsuits named as defendants several Musk companies and subsidiaries, including SpaceX, the social platform X, and SpaceX Super Intelligence, or SpaceXSI, the AI subsidiary of SpaceX.
SpaceXSI says it worked to curb creation of sexualised content
In a statement, SpaceXSI said sexual content involving minors, “whether real or AI-generated, is abhorrent. It has no place on X or in Grok, and neither do explicit images of real people made without their consent”.
If users try to break its safeguards to generate nonconsensual content, the company said, it takes “appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement”.
“Attempting to create this material is a serious crime and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors,” the statement said.
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. Photo: Getty Images / AFP
The lawsuits come at a time of growing concern about AI’s risks for children, from its impact on brain development to the unhealthy relationships many young people have formed with chatbots.
Grok, which can be accessed through Musk’s social media platform X, rolled out image generation and editing features to all users in December 2025, according to the Virginia lawsuit. By January, the tool had sparked a global backlash after it became clear Grok users could create realistic-looking but fake sexualised images of people. Researchers warned that some appeared to depict children.
As the Virginia lawsuit put it, “X was flooded with sexualised content – primarily of women”.
Lawsuits say company misled the world about its efforts
At least two countries, Malaysia and Indonesia, announced temporary bans, and other nations said they were launching or widening investigations. In response, Grok prevented nonpaying users from generating or editing images.
The change did not stop users from making more nonconsensual sexualised images; “it simply made that generation profitable”, Virginia’s lawsuit said.
The developer of Grok, which was then known as xAI, has since rebranded as SpaceX Super Intelligence.
Virginia argued that most major AI developers designed their products so they could not be used to produce sexualised images to avoid the generation of non-consensual content.
“Defendants declined to implement these safeguards. Defendants’ published system prompt materials – the set of instructions that guides the AI model’s behaviour – told Grok to ‘assume good intent’, stated that terms such as ‘teenage’ or ‘girl’ do not necessarily imply underage, and imposed minimal restrictions on sexual content,” the lawsuit said.
US President Donald Trump (left) and Musk at the White House in Washington on September 29,. Photo: Reuters
The lawsuit noted that xAI marketed Grok from the outset as a tool that would “answer spicy questions that are rejected by most other AI systems”.
And it argued X made “false, deceptive or misleading” statements in January about changes intended to prevent Grok from allowing users to edit images of real people in revealing clothes.
Users could still create nonconsensual sexualised imagery through a stand-alone app and website, the lawsuit said. And when users openly traded “jailbreak” prompts to get around what limits Grok did have on sexualised images, Musk’s companies failed to promptly address the exploits, the Virginia lawsuit alleged.
In its statement, SpaceXSI said it tests and adjusts protections “as abusers change tactics”.
The company has also brought at least three federal lawsuits against users it accuses of abusing the platform to create nonconsensual sexually explicit images and child sexual abuse material.
States sued under consumer protection laws
Both lawsuits draw heavily on news outlets’ investigative reporting about the roll-out of the tool, the backlash and the company’s response to it.
Virginia’s lawsuit, filed in a state court in Richmond, argued that the Musk companies violated the state’s consumer protection law by “misrepresenting that they implemented and enforced safeguards to protect consumers from exposure” to harmful sexualised imagery on their platforms.
It asked the court for US$2,500 for each “wilful violation” of the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, with an exact number to be proven at trial.
It also asked a judge to prevent the companies from further violating the consumer protection laws and force the defendants to give up any “ill-gotten gains” acquired in connection with the alleged violations.
The Oregon lawsuit makes a similar request.
“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritised growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable,” Jones said in a statement.
By Associated Press

title_en: Jensen Huang’s stunning return in 11 days – 5 key takeaways
content_en:
Donald Trump’s personal intervention can’t hide a divided administration as bipartisan US lawmakers vow to take action against shock move.
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO after US President Donald Trump said he weighed in directly with Nvidia’s board to support Huang's rehiring. Photo: Reuters
Jensen Huang’s dramatic return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday, engineered through US President Donald Trump’s personal intervention, carries major implications for Washington’s AI policy, priorities within the administration and its rivalry with Beijing.
What began with US media reports of his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, quickly morphed into a wider saga involving spying allegations, suspected AI chip smuggling to China, tighter export controls and infighting inside the Trump administration.
Here are the key takeaways from Huang’s exit, his stunning comeback and the broader saga.
1. A divided administration
Huang’s resignation and his quick return exposed a major rift within the Trump administration, with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly criticising the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to act against Megaspeed despite pressure from key US agencies. The two have long been wary of each other.
[embedded media]
On Sunday, Bessent told CBS News the administration had not yet received satisfactory answers from Nvidia about alleged illegal chip sales.
“We do need answers,” he said. “We will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top?”
The controversy also signalled a breakdown in inter-agency coordination, with the US Commerce Department using unprecedented language when releasing new export rules to cut off Chinese firms from remote access to advanced US AI chips.
Its Bureau of Industry and Security said the rules were written by the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, not Commerce itself.
Amid the finger-pointing, Trump backed Lutnick, saying last week that he had not “lost confidence” in him.
2. Trump keeps ‘China hawks’ at bay, for now
Despite calls from lawmakers and administration officials for tough action against Nvidia and Huang over smuggling and spying claims, Trump has pushed back on the narrative, doubting Alice Huang was a spy and backing exports of “older” H200 chips to China.
“As far as the woman is concerned, every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy,” Trump told CNBC on Monday.
[embedded media]
He added that he spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping about Huang at “length” during last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen.
The New York Times earlier reported that US Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio oversaw a memo earlier this year warning top officials that Huang was close to the alleged Chinese spy.
Rubio has repeatedly declined to comment on his role in the controversy.
Beijing has rejected the allegations, calling them “nothing but a smear against China”.
Trump “thinks Xi is his friend,” said Josh Rogin, author of the 2021 book Chaos Under Heaven: Trump, Xi, and the Battle for the 21st century.
“He has never been a China hawk,” he posted on social media.
3. Lawmakers vow to act
Several lawmakers from both parties have criticised the move to bring Huang back.
“This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and Nvidia still owe Congress answers,” said Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat likely to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January.
Democrat Elizabeth Warren says that Huang and Nvidia “still owe Congress answers”. Photo: Reuters
“It’s a smash-and-grab, with some deeply serious questions about Chinese Communist Party influence,” Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, wrote on social media.
“Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?” asked Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah.
Huang is scheduled to appear before multiple House committees on December 1 and the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.
Lawmakers from both parties are also pushing to attach a package of export-control bills to the annual National Defence Authorisation Act to further tighten restrictions on AI chip sales to China.
4. Message to Beijing
While the Commerce Department rolled out fresh export curbs following the Nvidia scandal, broader administration action against China remains uncertain.
China opposed the controls, calling them an “abuse of export control measures”, but hasn’t announced retaliatory measures yet.
“For Beijing, the Nvidia saga was not just about AI,” said George Chen, a Partner and Chair of Digital Practice at The Asia Group.
“It was further evidence that betting on Trump remains the most effective way to manage relations with Washington,” he wrote in a Substack post.
“The lesson Chinese policymakers are likely drawing is neither subtle nor complicated: Donald Trump remains the most influential political figure in America and, in many respects, the most consequential variable in the trajectory of US-China relations.”
[embedded media]
5. Tech executives too big to fail in AI race
The controversy also underscored a deeper dilemma over the centrality of Nvidia and Huang to America’s AI future – and how that dependence shapes its rivalry with China.
Under Huang, Nvidia poured tens of billions of dollars into AI firms that buy its hardware, a circular investment strategy he championed to make the company indispensable to US AI ambitions.
Critics initially welcomed Huang’s departure as a consequence of allegations that Nvidia’s chips aided China’s AI rise. Yet supporters now hail his reinstatement as vital to keeping Washington ahead of Beijing.
Trump echoed that view on Monday.
“Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you they would give him whatever he wanted,” Trump said.
“I know what President Xi is thinking because I would be thinking like, why don’t we make a deal with Jensen? We don’t have to bother with all the stuff. We don’t need spies. Let’s hire Jensen.”
By Nayan Seth
